summary: Describes how to negotiate Robust Header Compression on IP datagrams over PPP, by defining extensions to the PPP control protocols for IPv4 and IPv6. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Packet headers are long, like writing your full address on every postcard. Compression shortens them. This lets two ends of a phone-line link agree to do that.

subtitle: How two ends of a PPP link agree to squeeze IP packet headers with ROHC, using a new option in IPCP and IPV6CP.

tldr.problem: ROHC can compress IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers, but two ends of a PPP link first need a way to agree on how it will be used.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a ROHC configuration option for the IPv4 and IPv6 network control protocols (IPCP and IPV6CP) carrying MAX_CID, MRRU, MAX_HEADER and a PROFILES suboption, plus two new PPP protocol field values for small-CID and large-CID ROHC packets.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 1332 so that several IP-Compression-Protocol options can be offered at once. It has since been updated by RFC 4815.

today: RFC 3241 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1332 and has itself been updated by RFC 4815. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: ROHC Meets PPP
sections.content:
Robust Header Compression (ROHC), defined in RFC 3095, compresses the headers of IPv4 and IPv6 packets. Its first version focuses on RTP streams while also supporting other UDP flows, and it is a framework where more header compression profiles can be plugged in.

Before a PPP link can carry compressed headers, both ends must agree on parameters. PPP handles this with network control protocols (NCPs), and because there is one for IPv4 (IPCP) and one for IPv6 (IPV6CP), this RFC defines a configuration option for both.

ROHC assumes the link delivers packets in sequence. PPP normally does not reorder packets, but with mechanisms such as multiclass multilink PPP, care must be taken that packets sharing a compression context are not reordered.
sections.plainLanguage: Before two walkie-talkies can use short codes, they have to agree on the codes. PPP already has a way for two ends to talk about settings, and this RFC adds the settings for header compression.

sections.title: The Compression Option and Multiple Instances
sections.content:
The RFC adds a new compression protocol value for the IPCP IP-Compression-Protocol option from RFC 1332. As in that RFC, the option describes what the sender of a Configure-Request can receive, so each end must request it separately if compression is wanted in both directions.

RFC 1332 could be read as allowing only one compression protocol at a time. With ROHC it may be useful to combine RFC 2507 TCP compression with RFC 3095 RTP/UDP compression, so this document updates RFC 1332 to explicitly allow multiple instances of the option, each with a different IP-Compression-Protocol value and its own parameters.

Older implementations would most likely Configure-Nak or Configure-Reject the duplicate option, or accept the one they understand. To help interoperability, a peer implementing this RFC SHOULD react to a Configure-Nak or Configure-Reject by reducing the number of options offered to one.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally you may only name one code book. Now you can say "I can read both this book and that book", and the other side picks what it knows.

sections.title: The ROHC Option and PROFILES Suboption
sections.content:
The option has Type 2, a Length of at least 10, and an IP-Compression-Protocol value of 0003 (hex). Then come three 16-bit parameters and optional suboptions.

  • MAX_CID: the maximum context identifier value. It must be between 0 and 16383, where 0 means one context. The suggested value is 15.
  • MRRU: the maximum reconstructed reception unit. The suggested value is 0.
  • MAX_HEADER: the largest header size in octets that may be compressed. The suggested value is 168 octets, and it should be large enough to cover at least the outer network layer header.

The four profiles in RFC 3095 do not use MAX_HEADER, so it has no effect on them. Other profiles, for example ones based on RFC 2507, can make use of it by referencing it.

Suboptions each have a type, a length covering the whole suboption, and parameters. The PROFILES suboption (type 1, length 2n+2) MUST be supplied. It lists, in ascending order, n octet-pairs naming the ROHC profiles the decompressor supports. Most initial implementations of ROHC implement profiles 0x0000 to 0x0003.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a little form with blanks: how many conversations can be remembered, how big a header can be shortened, and which code books you know.

sections.title: One Channel for Two NCPs
sections.content:
ROHC can compress packets whose outer header is IPv4 or IPv6, and both IPCP and IPV6CP can negotiate its options. The negotiated capability applies to packets whose outer header matches the NCP it was negotiated for: an outer IPv6 header MUST NOT be sent if the option was not negotiated for IPV6CP.

Even so, the two NCPs together form exactly one ROHC channel. If the values differ, the channel uses the logical union: the maximum for MAX_CID, MRRU and MAX_HEADER, and the union of the two profile sets. Those values are kept even if one NCP is taken down. The context identifier space is shared by IPv4 and IPv6 headers and by small-CID and large-CID packets, so the compressor allocates identifiers from a common pool.

Taking down one NCP while the other stays open leaves contexts active, and the same holds if both are taken down and one or more is reopened. Taking down LCP destroys the channel, and reopening LCP and then IPCP or IPV6CP restarts ROHC with all contexts in no-context state. Feedback for the channel goes to the channel in the reverse direction on the same PPP link.
sections.plainLanguage: Two phone lines, one for old-style addresses and one for new-style, share one set of notebooks. Hanging up one line does not erase the notebook, but hanging up the main call does.

sections.title: Demultiplexing and Usage Details
sections.content:
ROHC has a header format with a small-CID variant (zero or one bytes identify the context) and a large-CID variant (one or two bytes). To keep PPP packets self-describing, the RFC defines two PPP Data Link Layer Protocol Field values: 0003 (hex) for ROHC small-CIDs and 0005 (hex) for ROHC large-CIDs.

A sender may use either format at any time, so the LARGE_CIDS parameter from RFC 3095 is not used, and every receiver MUST handle both. All CIDs within one ROHC packet MUST be the same size as the protocol field indicates, including embedded feedback. All packets that contribute to a segment MUST use the same protocol value, and a unit reconstructed from packets with different values MUST be discarded.

The ROHC uncompressed profile is not needed, because uncompressed packets can always be sent using normal PPP demultiplexing. Profile 0x0000 must still not be rejected, so all receivers MUST implement it.

For the RFC 3095 constants k_1, n_1, k_2 and n_2, the text says that because PPP links usually run with strong error detection, k_1 = n_1 = k_2 = n_2 = 1 is usually a good set of values.
sections.plainLanguage: Each envelope gets a stamp saying whether it uses short or long reference numbers, so the receiver never has to guess.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
Negotiating this option adds no security considerations beyond those of PPP, and the security considerations of ROHC apply. The RFC notes that header compression can, in rare cases, cause misdelivery of packets, so confidentiality should be assured by encryption if necessary.

Encryption at the IP layer, for example IPSEC, prevents compression of the encrypted headers, though the outer IP header and authentication or security headers can still be compressed. For RTP, full header compression remains possible if only the RTP payload is encrypted.

For IANA, new suboption identifiers use the Specification Required policy. The range 0 to 127 is reserved for IETF standard-track specifications, 128 to 254 is available for other specifications that meet the requirement, and 255 is reserved for future extensibility. Only identifier 1 (Profiles) is allocated here.
sections.plainLanguage: Short codes do not make secrets safer, and scrambling the whole letter hides the parts that would have been shortened. If something must stay secret, lock it separately.

fields.name: MAX_HEADER
fields.desc: Largest header size in octets that may be compressed.
